refurbishing-premises|restaurants-and-ho.h1: Refurbishment finance for restaurants and hospitality
refurbishing-premises|restaurants-and-ho.title: Refurbishment Finance for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
refurbishing-premises|restaurants-and-ho.desc: How restaurants, cafés, pubs and hotels finance a refit: kitchens, front of house and closure weeks. Get matched with one specialist finance broker. Free.
refurbishing-premises|restaurants-and-ho.lead: A refit in hospitality has to be paid for while the doors may be shut and the takings are low.
intro: Most hospitality refits are really two projects. Front of house, with new seating, lighting and a bar, is what guests see. The kitchen, with extraction, drainage, electrics and fire safety, is what keeps you open. The second often costs more than owners expect, and it sits behind walls and floors where surprises tend to turn up once the strip-out begins. Planning matters too, because a change of use, a new extraction flue or a licensing variation can add weeks before a single tile is laid.

The finance has to cover more than the invoices. If the site closes for two weeks, those weeks have rent, wages and suppliers but little income. A loan sized only to the contractor’s quote can leave the business short just as it reopens. Brokers often suggest sizing the amount to include trading lost during the works. Owners who phase the work across two or three quiet periods often borrow less at once, though the total cost can rise a little.
uses: Kitchen overhaul
Replace extraction, grease traps, flooring and cold rooms so the kitchen meets current rules and can handle more covers.
Pre-season refit
Close for a quiet fortnight in January or after the summer, then reopen with a new look before the busy period starts.
Bar and front of house
Rebuild a bar, move seating and upgrade lighting to raise the spend per head, often done in phases to avoid a full closure.
Adding rooms or a terrace
Convert a function room, fit out letting rooms above a pub or add an outdoor covered area that brings in trade all year.
fit: Card takings suit a merchant cash advance

Because most sales go through the till, a merchant cash advance can be repaid as a share of daily card takings, so repayments rise in busy weeks and ease in quiet ones. The cost is usually higher than a term loan, so it tends to suit smaller or faster projects. Lenders look at monthly card volume over the past year.
Unsecured loans for the larger job

An unsecured business loan, for example £60,000 over three or four years, spreads a full refit across the period the new fit-out will earn. Lenders look at accounts, bank statements and how much of your lease remains. Contractor quotes help for larger amounts.
Equipment can be financed separately

Ovens, chillers and coffee machines can often go on asset finance, which uses the equipment as security and keeps the main loan smaller. Owners of the freehold may also be able to borrow more through secured lending, using the building as security.
considerations: Lease length and landlord consent
A five-year loan on a site with three years left on the lease is a poor match. Check the lease, and get written consent for structural or shopfront changes before work starts.
Weather and seasonality
Repayments carry on through a wet January or a slow week after a bank holiday. Test the figures against your quietest months, not your best ones, before choosing a term.
Overruns and lost trade
Strip-outs commonly reveal old wiring, damp or drainage faults. A contingency in the amount, and an allowance for closure, is cheaper than a second round of borrowing halfway through.
faqs: Can I borrow to refit a rented restaurant?

Yes. Many tenants use unsecured business loans because there is no building to offer as security. Lenders will usually ask how long your lease has left and whether the landlord has agreed the works, so have both to hand before you apply. Landlord consent for structural or shopfront changes is also usually needed, so have it in writing before you apply.
Will lenders cover the weeks I am closed?

Often they will if the amount is built into the request. A broker may suggest adding a few weeks of fixed costs such as rent and core wages to the figure. Lenders will want to see a clear plan for the works and the reopening date. Closure costs can be included in the amount, but the lender will want to see that the business can still meet repayments if the reopening slips by a week or two.
Is a merchant cash advance good for a refit?

It can be for smaller projects, as repayments follow card takings. It is usually more expensive than a term loan, and a refit with a long closure produces no takings to repay from. A broker can compare both against your sales pattern. Where a closure is long, a plan that phases the work, keeping part of the venue open, usually suits repayments from takings better.
Can I finance kitchen equipment separately?

Frequently, yes. Ovens, extraction units and refrigeration are standard asset finance items, repaid over the equipment’s working life. Splitting the project this way keeps the general loan smaller and can make each lender’s decision simpler. Equipment finance is a separate decision from the building loan, so it can be arranged in parallel, often with a different lender who is comfortable with the equipment as security.
How much do hospitality businesses borrow for refits?

It varies widely. A café might borrow £15,000 to £40,000, while a restaurant with a full kitchen replacement or a pub adding rooms may need several times that. Loanleaf handles enquiries from £5,000 to £2m and above. Whatever the size, the amount is for the lender to assess against your accounts and bank statements, not a figure Loanleaf can promise.

paying-a-tax-bill|restaurants-and-hospit.h1: Tax bill finance for restaurants and hospitality
paying-a-tax-bill|restaurants-and-hospit.title: Tax Bill Finance for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
paying-a-tax-bill|restaurants-and-hospit.desc: How restaurants, cafés, pubs and hotels finance a VAT, PAYE or corporation tax bill that lands after a quiet spell. Get matched with a finance broker. Free.
paying-a-tax-bill|restaurants-and-hospit.lead: Hospitality tax bills often arrive just after the busy weeks have passed and the cash has gone.
intro: Hospitality has an awkward tax rhythm. A strong Christmas fills the till in December, but the VAT return covering it falls due in the quiet weeks of January and February, when suppliers and staff still need paying. Payroll is also the biggest cost in most venues, so PAYE and National Insurance run high every month, and a summer rush of temporary staff can push them higher. A venue with three or four sites can find that one site’s bill is covered while another’s is not, which makes the timing hard to manage from a single account.

Where a bill has to be met from a lean cash position, the choice is usually between asking HMRC for a payment plan and borrowing short term. A VAT and tax loan or a revolving credit facility can bridge the gap. The sensible question is how many months of takings it will take to repay, and whether those months are the quiet ones. Whichever route you take, it helps to know your quietest month before agreeing repayments, so that the instalment never lands on the week with the lowest takings.
uses: January VAT after Christmas
Settle the quarter that includes the festive trade, when the cash taken in December has already gone on stock, extra staff and tips.
Summer PAYE spike
Cover the payroll taxes for seasonal staff at a coastal, festival or tourist venue when the peak is over and bookings are tailing off.
Corporation tax after a good year
Pay a bill larger than expected after a strong year without drawing down the reserve held for a closure, repairs or a bad winter.
Several venues, one deadline
Meet VAT or PAYE for a small group when one site is struggling and the cash cannot simply be moved around.
fit: VAT and tax loans fit a fixed deadline

A VAT and tax loan is a short-term loan, often repaid over three to twelve months, where the lender pays HMRC or releases the money for the bill. For example, a restaurant with a £25,000 VAT bill might spread it over several months. Lenders look at recent returns, bank statements and the HMRC demand.
Revolving credit suits repeat peaks

If the same pressure comes back every quarter, a revolving credit facility gives a limit you draw on and repay as takings come in. You pay interest only on what you use, which suits a business whose cash cycle repeats through the year.
Seasonal repayment pattern matters

Agree repayments you can meet in your quietest month. A flat monthly payment is easier to plan, but some lenders may allow a different profile if the business is clearly seasonal. A broker can ask which ones do.
considerations: Compare with Time to Pay
HMRC may agree a payment plan directly, and for some venues that is cheaper than borrowing. HMRC charges interest on the balance, so compare the total cost of both routes.
Do not borrow for losses
If a venue is losing money each month, a tax loan only delays the problem. Lenders will see this in the accounts, and it is better to speak to your accountant first about the underlying position.
Tips, tronc and payroll
Tips and tronc arrangements affect payroll reporting, and mistakes here can cause surprise PAYE bills. Make sure your accountant has reconciled payroll before you decide how much to borrow.
faqs: Can a restaurant get a loan to pay VAT?

Yes. VAT and tax loans are designed for this. The lender either pays HMRC or releases funds so you can, and you repay in instalments over a few months. Lenders usually want the latest VAT return, accounts and bank statements. It is worth having the HMRC demand, the return and recent bank statements ready before you speak to anyone, because the lender will ask for all three.
Why does hospitality get caught out by VAT in January?

The quarter that includes December has the most sales, so it carries the largest VAT liability. It falls due after the busy trading has finished, at a time when income is lower and cash has already gone on stock and wages. Setting aside a fixed share of takings each week into a separate account can stop the same January pinch from repeating next year.
Is a revolving credit facility better than a tax loan?

It depends on whether this is a one-off or a pattern. A tax loan is a fixed amount repaid over a set period. A revolving facility stays available and you draw as needed, which suits repeat pressure. A broker can compare both. This can be an advantage for a venue with a steady monthly pattern, because a limit you can draw on is easier to plan around than a lump sum.
Can I borrow to pay PAYE for seasonal staff?

Lenders commonly consider PAYE and National Insurance alongside VAT and corporation tax. The aim is to pay HMRC in full and on time, then repay the lender over an agreed period. Evidence of your payroll and the HMRC demand will help. If wages run late or tips are paid out of the till, make sure payroll is recorded accurately first, as lenders will compare it to your bank statements.
What if my venue is already behind with HMRC?

Some lenders will only work with businesses that are up to date with tax. Others may consider it depending on the amount and circumstances. A broker can say which options are realistic, so you do not waste time on applications that will not proceed. Being behind does not always rule it out, but it narrows the choice, so speak to your accountant about the position before you apply.

refurbishing-premises|construction-and-t.h1: Refurbishment finance for construction and trades
refurbishing-premises|construction-and-t.title: Refurbishment Finance for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
refurbishing-premises|construction-and-t.desc: How builders, contractors and trades businesses finance a yard, workshop or office upgrade while jobs and retentions tie up cash. Free introduction to a broker.
refurbishing-premises|construction-and-t.lead: Builders spend their working lives improving other people’s premises, then find their own yard and office waiting.
intro: For a contractor or trades firm, premises means a yard, depot, workshop, storage unit or small office rather than a shopfront. The work is practical: new roller doors, secure racking, better lighting, a welfare cabin, hard standing that stops vans sinking in winter, or an office big enough for the estimators who now outnumber the desks. Many firms also find that a tidier, safer depot helps with tenders, because main contractors and insurers increasingly ask about security and site standards.

The challenge is that cash in this sector is usually committed to live jobs. Materials are bought ahead, wages are paid weekly, and retentions and slow-paying main contractors hold back money that is already earned. A refurbishment loan competes with all of that, which is why the amount and the timing matter as much as the rate. That is why firms often choose repayments they could meet even with one large payment running a month late, and keep the project small enough to stage.
uses: Secure yard and storage
Fence, gate and light the yard, add lockable stores and racking so tools and materials stop going missing.
Workshop upgrade
Rewire, add extraction, improve floor loading or fit a new bench layout for joinery, fabrication or electrical and plumbing assembly.
Welfare and office space
Add cabins or convert part of a unit for site managers and estimators, with meeting space where clients can be received.
Energy and running costs
Replace old heating, lights and roof insulation in a depot that is costing more to run each winter than it should.
fit: Unsecured loans for modest projects

An unsecured business loan, for example £35,000 over three years, suits a yard or workshop job where there is no property to charge. Lenders look at recent accounts, the order book and bank statements, and often ask how much work is committed for the next six months.
Secured lending where you own the site

If the business owns its yard or unit, secured business lending against the property may allow a larger amount over a longer term. Where a premises purchase is part of the plan, a commercial mortgage is the usual route, and a broker can say which structure fits.
Time the work to the quiet months

Many trades see work slow in December and January. Scheduling refurbishment then, and drawing the loan just before, avoids paying contractors out of money that is meant for wages and materials on a live job.
considerations: Retentions and payment terms
Five percent held for twelve months across several contracts adds up. Make sure repayments can be met even if a large payment is late, as lenders will test affordability against your bank statements.
Planning and the lease
Hard standing, cabins and new buildings may need planning permission, and an industrial unit lease may restrict alterations. Check both first.
Do the sums on doing it yourself
Many firms can use their own labour for part of the job. Borrow only for the materials and specialist trades you cannot supply, and keep records so a lender can see where the money went.
faqs: Can a trades business borrow to upgrade its yard?

Yes. Unsecured loans are common for yards and workshops, especially where the premises are rented. Owners of the site may be able to borrow more by offering it as security. Lenders look at your accounts, order book and bank statements. The lender will usually ask how long the lease has left and whether the landlord has agreed any structural work, so have both ready.
Do lenders worry about retentions?

They will see them in your accounts and cash flow. Retentions are normal in construction, but they can strain cash, so lenders may ask how much is outstanding and when it is due. A realistic repayment amount matters more than the headline figure. A lender will usually ask for a schedule of retentions held and due, so having that to hand shows you have considered the issue.
Should I use asset finance for machinery instead?

Equipment such as a CNC router, a compressor or a forklift usually goes on asset finance, which uses the item as security. Keeping that separate from the building work can keep the main loan smaller and each decision simpler. Cover for assets like these is arranged separately, which also lets the lender take the machine itself as security for that part.
How long should the loan run?

A common match is the useful life of the work. A security upgrade might be financed over two to three years, while a full building refit might run longer. Avoid a term longer than the time left on your lease. If you own the site, a longer term may be possible, but it should never run beyond the useful life of the work you are paying for.
Can I borrow while I have live contracts?

Yes, and lenders prefer to see an active order book. Be ready to show current contracts, work in progress and what has been invoiced. A broker can explain what a lender is likely to ask for given your mix of work. It also helps to have details of larger live jobs, because the lender is checking that repayments are covered by income already on the books.

paying-a-tax-bill|construction-and-trade.h1: Tax bill finance for construction and trades
paying-a-tax-bill|construction-and-trade.title: Tax Bill Finance for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
paying-a-tax-bill|construction-and-trade.desc: How builders and trades firms finance VAT, CIS-related and PAYE bills when client payments run late. Get matched with one specialist finance broker. Free.
paying-a-tax-bill|construction-and-trade.lead: In construction you can owe HMRC for work that your client has not yet paid you for.
intro: VAT is usually charged when you invoice, not when the customer pays, unless the business uses cash accounting, and it is paid with your return. A contractor can issue a £120,000 application in March, owe the VAT in the following quarter, and still be waiting for the client to pay. Add monthly PAYE and, for subcontractors, CIS deductions, and HMRC can be asking for money before the job has paid out. For a firm paid in monthly applications, this timing gap repeats every quarter, which is why the choice between a one-off loan and a standing facility matters so much.

There are two separate problems: the tax bill itself and the late payment that causes it. A VAT and tax loan deals with the first. Invoice finance deals with the second, by releasing cash against unpaid invoices. A good conversation with a broker usually starts by working out which of the two is actually hurting the business. Retentions and disputed final accounts make it worse, because they sit on the balance sheet as earned income that cannot yet be used to pay HMRC.
uses: VAT on unpaid applications
Pay the quarter’s VAT when large invoices raised in that period are still outstanding from the main contractor or developer.
PAYE after a busy few months
Cover payroll taxes after taking on extra labour for a large contract, before the final account is settled.
Corporation tax on a profitable year
Settle the bill after a good year when profit is tied up in work in progress and retentions rather than in the bank.
CIS and subcontractor payments
Meet monthly obligations when a contractor has paid subcontractors on time but has been paid late by its own client.
fit: VAT and tax loans for a defined bill

A VAT and tax loan pays a specific HMRC liability and is repaid over a few months. For example, £40,000 of VAT could be spread over six months. Lenders look at the VAT return, the HMRC demand and bank statements. They usually prefer to see that client contracts are real.
Invoice finance for the cause

Invoice finance releases a large part of an invoice soon after it is raised, which can clear the VAT bill and speed up wage payments. It suits contractors who bill other businesses on 30 to 60 day terms, and the lender will want to understand who your customers are.
Revolving credit for repeat gaps

If the shortfall comes up every quarter, a revolving credit facility lets you draw as needed and repay when the client pays. You pay interest on the amount used, which suits a business whose cash cycle varies with the jobs.
considerations: Ask about VAT cash accounting

Some businesses can account for VAT when they are paid rather than when they invoice, and the domestic reverse charge changes how VAT works on some building services. Your accountant can say what applies to you.
Retentions are not available cash
Money held as a retention is earned but cannot be spent. Lenders will treat it carefully, and so should you when working out what you can repay.
Borrowing is not the cure for late payers
If one client is paying months late, a loan covers the symptom. It is worth chasing, or reviewing the terms you offer, as well.
faqs: Can I get a loan to pay VAT if clients have not paid me?

Yes. VAT and tax loans are designed for this kind of timing gap. The lender will want to see the VAT return, the HMRC demand and evidence that the invoices are valid. Invoice finance may also help. It helps to include aged debtor reports and a list of the largest outstanding invoices, as lenders want to see who owes you and for how long.
Is invoice finance or a tax loan better for a contractor?

A tax loan fits a single bill. Invoice finance fits an ongoing gap between invoicing and being paid. Many contractors with regular late payments find invoice finance more useful, while a one-off bill points to a tax loan. A broker can compare them. Brokers often start by asking how long your invoices usually take to be paid, because that tells them which of the two options is likely to fit.
Do retentions affect my chances?

Lenders know retentions are normal. They will check how much is held and for how long, because it affects cash. A clear schedule of retentions due, alongside your accounts, helps a lender judge repayment capacity. It is useful to give the lender a list showing each retention, the contract it relates to and the expected release date, to show when the cash is due.
Can I finance PAYE and CIS-related bills?

Lenders commonly consider PAYE and National Insurance. Some will also look at other HMRC liabilities, depending on the case. The key point is that the lender is repaid from your trading, so a clear order book helps. Each lender has its own approach, so a broker can say which of them treat construction invoices and CIS arrangements in a way that suits your firm.
What should I have ready for a tax loan?

Usually your latest accounts, recent bank statements, the VAT return or HMRC demand, and details of major contracts. Starting a few weeks before the deadline gives you more options than waiting until the last few days. Lenders will also ask for details of the largest jobs, since they want to see that repayments are covered by income that is already contracted.

refurbishing-premises|retail.title: Refurbishment Finance for Retail Businesses | Loanleaf
refurbishing-premises|retail.desc: How shops and retailers finance a refit around stock buying, trading seasons and lease terms. Get matched with one specialist finance broker. Free to use.
refurbishing-premises|retail.lead: A shop refit has to be timed around stock buying, because both draw on the same pot of cash.
intro: A retailer deciding when to refit faces a problem most other sectors do not. The money for new shelving, flooring, lighting and a till area is the same money needed to buy stock for the next season. Refit in the autumn and the Christmas order may be squeezed. Refit in the spring and you risk reopening with thin shelves. Some retailers use the closure itself as a marketing event, announcing a reopening date so regular customers return quickly, which can shorten the dip in takings.

That is why many shop owners look for finance that is separate from working capital. The refit is paid for by a loan, and stock is bought from the cash the shop generates. The right structure depends on whether you rent or own, how steady your takings are and how long the new layout is expected to last before it needs changing again. Whichever route you choose, keep the refit budget and the stock budget separate on paper, so that an overrun on one does not quietly drain the other.
uses: Shopfront and window
Replace a tired fascia, signage and window display so the shop is noticed from the street and reflects the brand.
New layout and fixtures
Redesign the floor plan, add fixtures that fit new product ranges and improve the till area and queuing.
Moving to a larger unit
Fit out a bigger premises with the shelving, lighting and security needed before the first delivery arrives.
Click-and-collect and storage
Create a back room, collection point and stock area so online orders can be fulfilled from the shop.
fit: Unsecured loans for rented shops

An unsecured business loan, for example £45,000 over four years, is a common fit for a tenant refit. Lenders look at accounts, bank statements and the remaining lease, and larger amounts may need quotes from the shopfitter.
Merchant cash advance for card sales

Shops with heavy card takings may use a merchant cash advance, repaid as a share of daily card sales. It is usually more expensive than a term loan, and it suits retailers who want repayments to flex with footfall. It is less suited to a long closure with no sales.
Asset finance for fixtures and tills

Shelving, refrigeration, EPOS systems and security equipment can often be financed as assets. That keeps the main loan focused on the building work and spreads the cost of equipment over its useful life.
considerations: Time the work around trading

A four-week closure in the run up to Christmas can cost more in lost sales than the fit-out itself. Many retailers phase the work, or choose the quietest weeks, and build the lost income into what they borrow.
Lease and break clauses
A break clause or short remaining term makes a long loan risky. Match the term to how long you will use the new fit-out.
Do not use refit money for stock
Mixing the two makes it hard to see what the project cost. Keep a clear budget so you can judge whether the refit paid back.
faqs: Can a retailer borrow to refit a rented shop?

Yes. Unsecured loans are common because there is no property to offer. Lenders usually ask how long your lease has left and whether your landlord has agreed the works. Landlord consent for the works is also usually needed, particularly for shopfront, signage or structural changes, so it is worth getting that in writing early.
Is a merchant cash advance a good way to pay for a shop refit?

It can suit shops with strong card takings, as repayments follow sales. It tends to cost more than a loan, so a broker will usually compare it with a term loan. It is less helpful if the shop will be closed for weeks. A broker will compare the total repayable under each option, because a lower weekly cost can still mean more paid over the full term.
Can I include stock in the amount?

A general loan could, but it is often better to separate the two. Stock cycles and refit costs behave differently. A revolving credit facility may suit stock buying better, and a term loan the refit. Lenders will look at the whole picture, and a broker may suggest financing stock separately so the refit does not squeeze your next buying season.
Do lenders ask for the shopfitter’s quote?

For larger amounts, often yes. A written quote or cost breakdown shows what the money is for. For smaller amounts, lenders mostly look at your accounts and bank statements. It is sensible to get at least two quotes, because lenders and brokers will use them to judge whether the amount you are asking for is realistic.
How much do retailers borrow for refits?

A small independent shop may borrow £10,000 to £30,000, while a multi-site retailer or a large unit can need much more. Loanleaf handles enquiries from £5,000 to £2m and above. The amount depends on turnover, profit, your trading history and how much of the lease is left, and lenders decide each case on its merits.

paying-a-tax-bill|retail.h1: Tax bill finance for retail businesses
paying-a-tax-bill|retail.title: Tax Bill Finance for Retail Businesses | Loanleaf
paying-a-tax-bill|retail.desc: How shops and retailers finance VAT, corporation tax and PAYE bills that follow a stock-heavy peak season. Get matched with a specialist finance broker.
paying-a-tax-bill|retail.lead: Retail tax bills arrive after peak trading, when much of the takings are already sitting on the shelves as stock.
intro: Retailers collect VAT on every sale and hand most of it over a quarter later. After a strong autumn, that can be a large bill. The difficulty is that the cash taken in October and November is often already spent on January stock, rent and the staff who covered Christmas. The VAT is there on paper, but the money has moved on. Multi-site retailers have the added complication that stronger shops can mask weaker ones, so the group’s VAT bill may be larger than any single till suggests.

Corporation tax raises a similar issue. A profitable year can be tied up in unsold inventory, and the profit shown in the accounts is not all sitting in the bank. Short-term borrowing can spread the bill, though it is worth testing what the next two quarters of sales look like before taking it on. Before borrowing, many retailers check the stock position first, because selling slow lines at a small discount can release cash at lower cost than a loan.
uses: VAT after the Christmas quarter
Pay the quarter that includes the busiest trading when stock for the new year has already been bought.
Corporation tax with cash tied in stock
Settle a bill on profits that are held in inventory rather than the bank.
PAYE for seasonal staff
Cover payroll taxes for temporary staff taken on for peak weeks, once sales have tapered.
A bill across several shops
Meet a single HMRC deadline for a small group when only some shops have the cash on the day.
fit: A VAT and tax loan for the fixed bill

A VAT and tax loan is a short-term loan repaid over a few months, with the lender paying HMRC or releasing the funds for you to do so. For example, a retailer with a £30,000 VAT bill could repay over six months. Lenders look at VAT returns, accounts and bank statements.
Revolving credit for stock and tax together

Retailers with repeating peaks often prefer a revolving credit facility. You draw when needed, repay as sales come in, and pay interest only on what you use. It suits a business that has to cover both stock buying and tax from the same cash.
Repayments that follow sales
If sales are strongly seasonal, test repayments against the quietest quarter. A broker can ask lenders whether any will shape repayments to the pattern, though many use fixed monthly instalments.
considerations: Check which VAT scheme applies
Retailers can use special VAT schemes, and the choice affects how the bill is calculated. Your accountant can say whether the one you use is the best for the business.
Stock is not cash
A balance sheet with lots of stock looks strong, but lenders will focus on cash flow and sales. Be ready to show recent sales by month.
Look at the cause
If the bill keeps arriving when cash is short, consider setting aside VAT weekly in a separate account. A loan helps once, a habit helps every quarter.
faqs: Can a shop get a loan to pay VAT?

Yes. VAT and tax loans are designed for this. The lender either pays HMRC or releases funds to you, and you repay in instalments over several months. Expect to provide VAT returns, accounts and bank statements. Lenders will usually also ask for the HMRC demand and recent bank statements so they can see the bill and how your sales are performing.
Why does retail VAT feel hard to pay?

VAT on sales is collected with each sale, but the payment falls due after the quarter ends. If cash has gone on stock or rent in between, the money is no longer there. It is a timing issue more than a profit one. The gap between a sale and the VAT payment can run to several months, and in that time stock, rent and wages all draw on the same takings.
Is Time to Pay better than borrowing?

HMRC may agree a payment plan, and for some shops that costs less than borrowing. HMRC charges interest on what is outstanding. Compare the total cost and conditions of both before choosing. It is worth asking an adviser to work out the total interest under each route, as the cheaper monthly cost is not always the cheaper arrangement overall.
Can I borrow if my sales are seasonal?

Yes. Lenders see seasonal trading regularly in retail. They will look at the full year’s figures, not just recent months. A clear explanation of your peak and quiet periods helps. Strong seasonal peaks are not a problem in themselves, so long as the figures show that the business can meet repayments through the quieter months.
How soon should I start?

As early as you can. Lenders need time to run their checks and HMRC deadlines do not move. Starting a few weeks before the bill is due gives more choice than leaving it to the final days. A broker can also check which lenders are willing to proceed in the time you have, and which would be too slow for your deadline.

refurbishing-premises|manufacturing.title: Refurbishment Finance for Manufacturing Businesses | Loanleaf
refurbishing-premises|manufacturing.desc: How manufacturers finance factory floor, unit and workshop refurbishment without stopping production. Get matched with one specialist finance broker. Free.
refurbishing-premises|manufacturing.lead: A factory refurbishment is judged on how little production it costs, not just on what the building work costs.
intro: Manufacturers refurbish for reasons that are mostly operational. A floor that cannot take a heavier machine, lighting that is too dim for quality checks, a roof that leaks onto stock, or a layout that makes forklifts take the long way round. The work often has to be done around production, in sections, or over a shutdown. A phased plan, doing one bay at a time while the others keep producing, usually costs more in contractor time but protects output and customer deliveries.

That makes the cost two-sided. There is the contractor’s bill, and there is the output lost while a line is moved or a bay is out of use. Lenders tend to be more comfortable with refurbishment where the benefit is clear, such as a layout that raises throughput, or an energy upgrade that lowers running costs in a measurable way. Insurers sometimes drive the work too, by asking for fire separation or better storage, and a written recommendation from them can help explain the project to a lender.
uses: Floor and layout
Re-lay a floor, change bay layouts and move services so a new line or heavier machine can be installed.
Lighting and energy
Fit LED lighting, insulation and better heating to cut running costs and improve working conditions.
Health and safety work
Add extraction, fire separation, safer walkways and guarding after an inspection or insurer’s recommendation.
Clean areas and quality
Create a controlled or clean room, or a dedicated inspection area, to meet a customer’s quality requirements.
fit: Secured lending where you own the unit

Manufacturers that own their site can often borrow more, over longer, through secured business lending against the property. For example, £250,000 over ten years to refurbish a production hall. Lenders will value the property and look at the order book and accounts.
Unsecured loans for tenants

An unsecured business loan, for example £50,000 over four years, is often used where the site is rented. Lenders look at turnover, margins and customer concentration. A lease with several years left helps.
Keep machinery separate

New machines usually go through asset finance, which uses the machine as the security. Splitting the project this way keeps the building loan smaller and lets each piece of finance run for the life of what it pays for.
considerations: Downtime is a real cost
Include lost output in the budget. A shutdown planned around a quiet week or a holiday closure is cheaper than a rushed job in the middle of a large order.
Capital costs versus repairs
Some work improves the property and some simply repairs it. Your accountant can advise how each is treated, which may affect the tax position.
Be careful about long loans on short leases
If the lease has three years left, a ten-year term does not match. Check the lease, and ask the landlord about renewal before you commit.
faqs: Can a manufacturer borrow to refurbish a rented unit?

Yes. Unsecured loans are common for tenants, and lenders look at the remaining lease, accounts and order book. Landlord consent for the work is usually needed. Some landlords of industrial units are happy to contribute or reduce rent during works, so it is worth asking before you borrow the whole amount.
Will lenders want to see how the work improves output?

Often they will ask what the work is for. A clear plan showing the benefit, such as capacity, quality or lower energy costs, helps a lender understand the case, particularly for larger amounts. Include a short description of the project, the contractor’s quote and the date you expect to restart full production, which gives the lender a clear picture.
Can I finance a new line and the building work together?

Sometimes, but many brokers suggest splitting them. Asset finance suits the machinery, and a loan suits the building. Separate facilities can be easier to arrange and better matched to each item’s life. That way a mechanical breakdown or a payment delay on one facility does not affect the other, and each lender is secured on its own asset.
Does owning the unit help?

It can. Lenders may offer larger amounts or longer terms when a property can be offered as security. A commercial mortgage may also be an option for a purchase, depending on the case. It depends on the value of the property, existing borrowing against it and your trading figures, so a lender will normally arrange a valuation.
How long do manufacturers usually borrow for?

It varies. An energy or lighting project might run for two to five years, while a major building refit on an owned site can run longer. A broker can suggest a term that fits the project and the lease. Choosing a term shorter than the remaining lease, and no longer than the useful life of the work, is a sensible starting point.

paying-a-tax-bill|manufacturing.h1: Tax bill finance for manufacturing businesses
paying-a-tax-bill|manufacturing.title: Tax Bill Finance for Manufacturing Businesses | Loanleaf
paying-a-tax-bill|manufacturing.desc: How manufacturers finance VAT, PAYE and corporation tax bills when long customer payment terms and stock tie up cash. Free introduction to a broker.
paying-a-tax-bill|manufacturing.lead: Manufacturers pay for materials and wages first and are paid weeks later, so tax can land before the money does.
intro: A typical manufacturer buys raw materials, pays a team to make something over several weeks, ships it, and then waits 30, 60 or even 90 days for the customer to pay. During that time VAT on the sale becomes due on the invoice date in many cases, and PAYE and National Insurance fall due every month regardless. Because production runs are planned months ahead, a manufacturer can usually forecast its VAT and payroll quite accurately, which makes repayment planning easier than it is in other sectors.

Imports can add to the strain. Where materials come from abroad, import VAT may be due on arrival, though some businesses can account for it through their VAT return. Because every manufacturer is different, the right solution depends on whether the bill is a one-off, or a symptom of long terms that will cause the same squeeze again next quarter. A new large order can make the squeeze worse before it helps, since materials and labour are paid for months before the customer’s payment arrives.
uses: VAT before the customer pays
Meet a VAT return on large invoices raised in the quarter that customers have not yet settled.
Monthly PAYE on a large team
Cover payroll taxes in a month when materials have taken most of the cash, ahead of a big delivery.
Corporation tax after capital spending
Pay a bill on profits that have already been reinvested in stock, machinery or a new unit.
Import VAT on materials
Fund VAT on imported components when the bill arrives before the finished product is sold.
fit: A tax loan for a one-off bill

A VAT and tax loan is a short-term loan for a defined HMRC liability, usually repaid over a few months. For example, £60,000 of VAT could be repaid over six to nine months. Lenders look at accounts, VAT returns and the HMRC demand.
Invoice finance for the underlying gap

If the problem is long customer terms, invoice finance can release most of an invoice’s value once it is issued. It suits manufacturers selling to other businesses, and the lender will assess the customers’ quality and the spread of your sales.
Revolving credit for a repeat pattern
A revolving credit facility gives a limit that can be drawn and repaid as customers pay. It suits quarterly VAT and other regular pressure points, with interest charged on the amount used.
considerations: Concentration risk
If one customer makes up most of your sales, lenders may be cautious, particularly with invoice finance. Say so early and let the broker find lenders who accept it.
Check capital allowances with your accountant
Spending on machinery can change a corporation tax bill. Your accountant can explain what applies, which helps you borrow the right amount.
Do not use tax money for losses
If margins are thin and tax is only one pressure, a loan can delay the problem. Fix pricing or terms where you can.
faqs: Can a manufacturer get a loan to pay VAT?

Yes. VAT and tax loans are for this. The lender pays HMRC or releases funds, and you repay in instalments. You will usually need recent accounts, the VAT return and bank statements. It can also help to show the lender a simple forecast of VAT and payroll for the next two quarters, so it sees that this is a timing issue.
Would invoice finance be better than a tax loan?

If the pressure comes from long customer payment terms, invoice finance can help every month. A tax loan suits one defined bill. A broker can compare them against your sales and customers. Many manufacturers use both, with a revolving or invoice facility for day-to-day timing and a separate short loan for a larger one-off liability.
What about import VAT?

Lenders can consider import VAT as a tax liability, depending on the structure. Ask your accountant whether postponed VAT accounting applies to you, as it can reduce the timing problem. Where the claim is made through the return, the issue may be smaller than it first appears, but an accountant should confirm how it applies to your imports.
Does it matter if I have a large order book?

Yes. A strong order book shows future income, and lenders may be more comfortable. Be ready to show contracts, forecasts and the recent run of sales when you apply. Lenders will also ask about the quality of the customers behind the order book, as repayment depends on those customers paying you on time.
How early should I apply?

As early as possible. Lenders need time to complete checks, and tax deadlines are fixed. Starting a few weeks before the due date leaves you with more options than a last-minute request. A broker can check which lenders understand manufacturing cycles and are willing to proceed within the time you have before the bill is due.

refurbishing-premises|transport-and-logi.h1: Refurbishment finance for transport and logistics
refurbishing-premises|transport-and-logi.title: Refurbishment Finance for Transport and Logistics | Loanleaf
refurbishing-premises|transport-and-logi.desc: How haulage and logistics firms finance depot, yard, workshop and warehouse upgrades. Get matched with one specialist finance broker. Free to use.
refurbishing-premises|transport-and-logi.lead: For a haulier the premises is the operating base, so a refurbishment has to keep vehicles moving.
intro: Transport businesses spend heavily on vehicles and tend to leave the depot until last. Yet a failing yard surface damages tyres, a poorly lit workshop slows maintenance, and a cramped office limits the planners who keep the fleet busy. Depot upgrades also cover loading docks, wash bays, fuel storage, security gates and charging points for electric vans. Customers sometimes require upgraded facilities as a condition of a contract, so a refurbishment may be linked directly to winning or keeping work.

These are not quick jobs. Work on a yard or a dock interrupts movements, and operators usually need to plan around vehicle schedules and customer deliveries. Lenders see this sector often and are used to seeing it as asset-heavy, so a refurbishment loan is judged against the whole picture of fleet commitments, contracts and cash cycle. That is why lenders often ask for a full list of existing vehicle and equipment finance, alongside contracts, before they decide what is affordable on top.
uses: Yard resurfacing and drainage
Re-lay worn hard standing, fix drainage and add markings so heavy vehicles can manoeuvre safely.
Workshop upgrade
Install lifting equipment, inspection pits, better lighting and extraction so maintenance is done in-house.
Loading docks and warehouse
Add or repair dock levellers, doors and racking so vehicles are turned round more quickly.
Charging and fuel
Install EV charging, bunded fuel storage or a wash bay as the fleet changes or customers set requirements.
fit: Secured lending against the depot

Owners of their depot can often borrow through secured business lending against the property, with longer terms for larger projects. For example, £150,000 over eight years to rebuild a yard. Lenders look at the property value and the strength of the contracts.
Unsecured loans for tenants

Where the depot is rented, an unsecured business loan may suit smaller projects such as lighting, doors or an office refit. Lenders will check the lease length and landlord consent, plus your accounts and bank statements.
Vehicles stay on asset finance

Trucks, trailers and forklifts normally go through asset finance, repaid over their working life. Keeping refurbishment separate stops the building loan competing with hire purchase or lease payments on the fleet.
considerations: Fleet commitments come first
Lenders will look at existing hire purchase and lease payments. A refurbishment loan has to fit on top of those, so work out total monthly commitments before you borrow.
Planning, licensing and environment
Changes to yards, fuel storage and drainage can raise planning and environmental points, and an operator’s licence may refer to the operating centre. Check with the relevant bodies and your advisers.
Revenue during the works
If part of the yard is out of use, vehicle movements and loading may slow. Allow for the cost of any temporary arrangements.
faqs: Can a haulage firm borrow to upgrade its depot?

Yes. Owners can often use secured lending against the site, while tenants may use unsecured loans. Lenders look at accounts, contracts, existing commitments and how long the lease runs. Landlord consent is also needed for most changes to a leased yard or depot, and some leases restrict fuel storage and heavy alterations.
Should I put building work and vehicles in one loan?

Usually not. Vehicles suit asset finance, repaid over their life with the vehicle as security. Building work suits a loan or secured lending. Separating them keeps each simpler. Many operators find this split easier to manage, because the lender for each facility has the asset in front of it and can price it accordingly.
Do lenders worry about fuel prices and customer payment times?

They will consider them as part of the cash picture. Long customer payment terms and fuel costs affect cash flow. Invoice finance may be worth discussing if late payers are a regular problem. The lender will want to see that existing fleet payments are comfortably covered, since those commitments come before a new refurbishment loan.
Can I finance EV charging points?

Often, yes. Charging infrastructure can be financed as part of a general loan or as equipment, depending on the setup. A broker can suggest the best split for your fleet and site. Equipment suppliers sometimes offer finance for charging units, and a broker can compare that with a loan arranged separately before you commit.
How long does a depot loan usually run?

It depends on the work and on whether you own the site. Smaller projects often run three to five years, while a major rebuild on owned land can be longer. The term should not outlast your right to use the site. Many lenders will also look at whether a long lease or freehold gives you secure use of the site for as long as the loan runs.

paying-a-tax-bill|transport-and-logistic.h1: Tax bill finance for transport and logistics
paying-a-tax-bill|transport-and-logistic.title: Tax Bill Finance for Transport and Logistics | Loanleaf
paying-a-tax-bill|transport-and-logistic.desc: How haulage and logistics firms finance VAT, PAYE and corporation tax bills when customers pay on 30 to 60 day terms. Free introduction to a broker.
paying-a-tax-bill|transport-and-logistic.lead: Hauliers pay drivers and fuel up front, then wait on customers, so a tax bill can fall in the gap.
intro: A haulage firm’s costs arrive fast. Drivers are paid weekly or monthly, fuel is bought every day, and vehicles need servicing and tyres. Customers, however, often pay on 30 to 60 day terms. VAT on those invoices is usually due before the money arrives, and PAYE and National Insurance on a large driver payroll fall due every month. Fuel is the other pressure, because the price can move sharply between quarters while the rate agreed with customers stays fixed for months.

VAT can also swing. A big vehicle purchase may produce a refund one quarter, then a larger bill the next. Fuel carries VAT that can be reclaimed, which makes the figure harder to predict. For this reason, many operators plan around cash rather than around the tax return, and borrow only for the weeks when the two do not match. Operators with a few large customers can feel it most, since one late payer can delay a very large share of the month’s income.
uses: VAT while customers pay late
Pay the quarter’s VAT while large invoices to retailers or manufacturers remain unpaid.
Driver payroll taxes
Cover PAYE and National Insurance in a month when fuel and repairs have taken more cash than planned.
Corporation tax after fleet growth
Settle a bill on a profitable year when profits are already committed to new vehicles and finance payments.
A quiet-month shortfall
Bridge a tax deadline that falls just after a slow period, such as the weeks after a seasonal peak.
fit: Invoice finance addresses the gap

Invoice finance releases much of an invoice soon after it is raised, and is widely used in haulage because customers pay on terms. It can help meet VAT and payroll without a separate loan. The lender will review your customers and how you bill.
A tax loan for a one-off bill

A VAT and tax loan is repaid over a few months and suits a defined bill. For example, a firm with a £35,000 VAT bill might spread it over six months. Lenders look at VAT returns, the HMRC demand, accounts and bank statements.
Revolving credit for fluctuating weeks

A revolving credit facility lets you draw and repay as the cash cycle changes. It suits fleets with uneven weeks, as interest is charged only on what you use. Lenders consider turnover, accounts and existing commitments.
considerations: Existing finance payments
Many operators already pay hire purchase and lease costs on vehicles. A lender will count these, so check total commitments before adding a new one.
Customer concentration
If a few customers make up most of your sales, say so. Some lenders are comfortable with it and others are not.
Ask about VAT schemes
Your accountant can advise whether a different VAT scheme would reduce the timing problem, which may mean you borrow less.
faqs: Can a haulier get a loan to pay VAT?

Yes. VAT and tax loans are designed for this, and the lender pays HMRC or releases funds so you can. You repay over several months. Expect to provide VAT returns, accounts and bank statements. The lender will usually also want to see your aged debtors report, because it shows who owes you money and how late each customer typically pays.
Is invoice finance common in transport?

Yes. Many hauliers use it because customers pay on terms while costs are due immediately. It can free cash that helps with tax, fuel and payroll. A broker can explain how it would work with your customers. It is worth asking whether the facility can grow with your sales, since a larger fleet will mean a larger gap between costs and payments.
Will existing vehicle finance affect my chances?

Lenders will take it into account. Hire purchase and lease payments are a fixed commitment, so they check that a new repayment is affordable. Clear figures on your monthly outgoings help a lender decide. Most lenders will want to see how much is already committed each month to vehicles and premises, so have those figures ready for the broker.
Can I borrow to pay PAYE for drivers?

Lenders commonly consider PAYE and National Insurance alongside VAT and corporation tax. The aim is to pay HMRC on time and repay the lender over an agreed period. A broker can ask lenders whether they will work with the invoice mix and the customers you currently serve before you commit to an application.
What if I need the money quickly?

Some lenders can move in days once they have documents, but it is safest not to depend on that. Having accounts, bank statements and the HMRC demand ready, and starting early, gives the best chance of meeting the deadline. If the deadline is close, tell the broker straight away, as it may shape which lenders are worth approaching and how you present your case.

refurbishing-premises|healthcare-and-den.h1: Refurbishment finance for healthcare and dental
refurbishing-premises|healthcare-and-den.title: Refurbishment Finance for Healthcare and Dental | Loanleaf
refurbishing-premises|healthcare-and-den.desc: How dental practices, clinics and care providers finance surgery refits, treatment rooms and compliance work. Get matched with a specialist finance broker.
refurbishing-premises|healthcare-and-den.lead: Practices refit treatment rooms to meet standards and add capacity, usually without wanting to turn patients away.
intro: A surgery is not an ordinary room. Treatment rooms need washable surfaces, suitable plumbing, ventilation, lighting and careful separation of clean and dirty areas. Dental practices work to guidance on decontamination, and clinics and care providers have inspection standards of their own. A refurbishment is often triggered by an inspection, a new clinician needing a room, or equipment that no longer fits. Many practices schedule works over a bank holiday weekend or a planned closure, so that only a few appointments are lost.

Income in this sector tends to be steady, with regular patients and, for some practices, recurring contracts. That makes it easier to plan repayments, but closed rooms still mean lost appointments. Many practices refit one room at a time, so the practice keeps trading, and size the loan around a phased programme rather than a single large project. A new room also carries running costs, such as an extra nurse or reception cover, which should be included when you test whether repayments are affordable.
uses: New surgery or treatment room
Convert a spare room, fit services and flooring and add the equipment to open another chair or consulting room.
Decontamination and compliance work
Rebuild a sterilisation area or upgrade ventilation and surfaces to meet current guidance.
Reception and waiting area
Refit the front of the practice for accessibility, privacy and a better first impression for patients.
Moving to larger premises
Fit out new premises with plumbing, compressors, cabling and the layout that a clinical team needs.
fit: Unsecured loans for phased refits

An unsecured business loan, for example £80,000 over five years, suits a surgery refit where the practice rents its building. Lenders look at accounts, patient numbers and the lease. Clinical practices with steady income are generally easy for lenders to understand.
Asset finance for clinical equipment

Dental chairs, X-ray units, autoclaves and scanners are classic asset finance items, repaid over the equipment’s useful life. Splitting equipment from building work keeps each facility matched to the item it pays for.
Commercial mortgages for owners

Practice owners buying or refinancing premises may look at a commercial mortgage, and secured lending can fund larger works on a building the practice already owns. Lenders will value the property and check profitability.
considerations: Lost appointments during works
Closed rooms mean fewer appointments. A phased plan, or work done over a bank holiday, limits the impact and makes repayments easier to cover.
Regulation and sign-off
Clinical premises may need sign-off or notification when major changes are made. Check what applies with the relevant regulator and your adviser before work begins.
Lease and goodwill
If you plan to sell the practice, a lender and a buyer will want to know the lease is secure. Short leases limit how much you should spend.
faqs: Can a dental practice borrow to refit its surgery?

Yes. Many practices use unsecured business loans for building work and asset finance for equipment. Lenders look at accounts, patient volumes, the lease and whether the practice is owned or rented. Lenders will usually ask for the lease, the contractor’s quote and your latest accounts, so it helps to gather them before applying.
Should I finance equipment separately?

Often, yes. Chairs, scanners and sterilisers are suited to asset finance, with the equipment as the security. A separate loan then covers building work, which keeps each facility matched to what it pays for. Compressors, scanners and chairs also keep a resale value, which can help the lender decide how to structure the finance for them.
Do lenders like healthcare businesses?

Many see steady income and repeat patients as a positive. The assessment still depends on your accounts, borrowing, profitability and ability to repay, so there are no promises. A broker can say which lenders know the sector. It varies by lender and does not guarantee any result, because each decision depends on your own accounts, borrowing and repayment ability.
Can I borrow if I only own the practice, not the building?

Yes. Many practices rent premises and use unsecured loans. The lease length matters, as does landlord consent for the work, and lenders will usually ask for both. Landlord consent for works that touch plumbing or structure is usually essential, and lenders will want to see it before releasing the amount.
How much do practices typically borrow?

A single surgery refit might need £30,000 to £100,000 including equipment, while a full practice move or a new multi-chair site can be several times that. Loanleaf handles enquiries from £5,000 to £2m and above. Lenders decide each case on its merits, taking into account your accounts, existing borrowing and the lease or ownership position.

paying-a-tax-bill|healthcare-and-dental.h1: Tax bill finance for healthcare and dental
paying-a-tax-bill|healthcare-and-dental.title: Tax Bill Finance for Healthcare and Dental | Loanleaf
paying-a-tax-bill|healthcare-and-dental.desc: How dental practices, clinics and care providers finance corporation tax, PAYE and VAT bills. Get matched with one specialist finance broker. Free to use.
paying-a-tax-bill|healthcare-and-dental.lead: Healthcare tax bills are shaped by large payrolls and by VAT rules that differ from most other businesses.
intro: Healthcare providers have a distinct tax profile. Many clinical services are VAT exempt, so a practice may have little or no output VAT on its main work, while still being unable to reclaim VAT on what it buys. Practices that also sell taxable services, such as some cosmetic treatments, may have a mixed position that deserves close attention from an accountant. Practices with associates or locums should check that those payments are treated correctly for tax, since errors here can create bills that nobody planned for.

The larger pressures are often payroll and corporation tax. Clinicians, nurses and reception staff mean heavy PAYE and National Insurance each month, and a profitable year can produce a sizeable corporation tax bill. Income from NHS contracts and regular patients is often steady, which helps repayments, but the date the bill falls due may not line up with when payments arrive. Because income is often predictable, a lender can see repayments more clearly, though the assessment still depends on your accounts and existing commitments.
uses: Corporation tax after a strong year
Pay a bill on profits that have already gone into equipment, refurbishment or buying out a partner.
Payroll taxes on a large team
Meet PAYE and National Insurance in a month when contract payments are due later than the payroll run.
VAT on taxable services
Cover quarterly VAT where a practice sells taxable services alongside exempt clinical work.
Associate and locum costs
Smooth a tax deadline in a month where payments to associates or locums have taken a larger share of cash.
fit: VAT and tax loans for a clear bill

A VAT and tax loan is a short-term loan for a defined HMRC bill, repaid over a few months. For example, a practice with a £50,000 corporation tax bill might spread it over eight months. Lenders look at accounts, the HMRC demand and bank statements.
Unsecured loans for flexibility

A general unsecured business loan can pay a tax bill and be repaid over a longer period, for example two or three years. This costs more overall, but monthly payments are smaller, which may suit a practice with steady income.
Revolving credit for uneven months
A revolving credit facility suits practices with irregular payment dates, as you draw when needed and repay when funds arrive. You pay interest on the amount used, and the limit stays available.
considerations: Check your VAT position
Partial exemption rules can be complex, and a mistake can lead to unexpected bills. Your accountant can confirm what applies before you decide how much to borrow.
Personal tax is separate
Directors’ and partners’ personal tax is a personal liability, not a company bill, so business finance is not the route for it.
Keep clinical income steady
If a tax loan reduces monthly cash, consider whether it affects hiring or equipment plans. Weigh repayments against what the practice has committed to.
faqs: Can a dental practice get a loan to pay corporation tax?

Yes. VAT and tax loans cover corporation tax as well as VAT and PAYE. The lender pays HMRC or releases funds so you can, and you repay over an agreed period. Expect to provide accounts and bank statements. Lenders will usually ask for the HMRC demand and recent bank statements, so a practice that keeps good records tends to move faster.
Is healthcare VAT exempt?

Many clinical services are exempt, but not all. Cosmetic and some private services may be taxable, and exemption can limit VAT you can reclaim. Check your position with an accountant, as the rules depend on what you provide. A short conversation with your accountant before you borrow will confirm how much of the bill is VAT and how much is another tax.
Will NHS income help my application?

Regular, contracted income can help a lender understand cash flow, though no outcome is guaranteed. Lenders still look at accounts, borrowing and profitability. A broker can explain how your income is likely to be viewed. Contracts and recurring patient income can show lenders how cash arrives, but they are one part of a wider review of your finances.
Can I spread a PAYE bill?

Lenders commonly consider PAYE and National Insurance. HMRC may also agree a payment plan directly, and the total costs of both routes can differ, so compare them before deciding. A payment plan may be possible for some, and for others borrowing to pay in full is simpler, so compare the total cost and the conditions.
What if I bought another practice recently?

Acquisition debt is part of the picture. Lenders will look at what you already owe and whether the practice can carry additional repayments. Clear figures on income and borrowing help a broker find suitable lenders. Be open with the broker about what you owe and why, as lenders prefer a clear explanation to surprises discovered during their checks.

refurbishing-premises|ecommerce.title: Refurbishment Finance for Ecommerce Businesses | Loanleaf
refurbishing-premises|ecommerce.desc: How online sellers finance warehouse, studio, office and showroom fit-outs as they outgrow a spare room or unit. Get matched with a specialist finance broker.
refurbishing-premises|ecommerce.lead: Online businesses refurbish when the stock outgrows the space, and the unit becomes the bottleneck.
intro: Few ecommerce firms have glossy premises. They have a unit, a warehouse bay or a converted barn full of boxes, and refurbishment means making it work harder. That can be racking and a mezzanine floor, packing benches, a photography studio, a returns area, or heating and lighting so people can work there in winter. Insurers and building control may also have a say on racking, mezzanines and fire exits, so it is worth getting their view before the project starts.

The reasons are practical. Order volumes rise, the picking route gets longer, and mistakes creep in. Because most of the money in an online business goes on stock and advertising, premises spending tends to be squeezed until it becomes a problem. Lenders will usually ask for sales history from your store or marketplace, and how much of it repeats. A refit can pay back through fewer picking errors and faster dispatch, but it helps to put a figure on that before borrowing, because a lender may ask.
uses: Racking and mezzanine
Add racking and a mezzanine floor so more stock fits in the same footprint and picking is faster.
Packing and returns area
Fit benches, labelling stations and a separate returns zone so orders and refunds stop sharing the same space.
Photography and content studio
Build a lit studio with backdrops and storage for product shots, so content is produced in-house.
Showroom or collection point
Fit out a small trade counter or showroom, where customers can collect orders or see products.
fit: Unsecured loans for fit-outs

An unsecured business loan, for example £30,000 over three years, can pay for building work in a rented unit. Lenders look at sales history from your website and marketplaces, accounts and bank statements, and may ask how steady repeat sales are.
Asset finance for racking and machinery

Racking, conveyors, label printers and packing machines can often be financed as assets. That keeps the main loan focused on the building work and spreads the cost over the working life of the equipment.
Revolving credit for stock alongside

Stock buying and refurbishment compete for cash. A revolving credit facility for stock, with a separate term loan for the fit-out, can stop one starving the other. A broker can explain how to split them.
considerations: Lease terms on industrial units
Industrial leases often restrict alterations, and a mezzanine can raise building control and insurance points. Check the lease and ask the landlord before ordering.
Sales that depend on a platform
If most sales come from one marketplace, lenders may ask how exposed you are to changes there. Show your wider customer base and repeat orders if you can.
Is it the right fix?
A larger unit or a third-party warehouse may suit better than a refit. Compare the cost of improving the current space with moving or outsourcing.
faqs: Can an ecommerce business borrow to fit out a warehouse?

Yes. Unsecured loans are common for tenants. Lenders will want to see accounts and sales history from your website or marketplaces, plus bank statements and the lease. Landlord consent and the lease terms are usually checked as well, since changes to an industrial unit often need the landlord’s agreement.
Do lenders accept marketplace sales as evidence?

Often they do. Reports from your store or marketplace, alongside bank statements and accounts, can show trading history. A broker will explain what a lender is likely to ask for. It helps to download several months of sales and payout reports, as they show trading history in a form that lenders find easy to follow.
Is asset finance suitable for racking?

Typically yes, because racking, conveyors and packing equipment are physical assets. Financing them separately keeps the main loan smaller and matches repayments to the life of each item. A lender can then secure the loan against the equipment itself, which can help where you have few other assets to offer.
Should I use a loan or a revolving facility?

A term loan suits a fixed project with a known cost. A revolving credit facility suits fluctuating cash needs such as stock. Many online sellers use both for different purposes. Some sellers start with a modest loan for the fit-out and add a revolving facility later, once the new layout is working as planned.
How much do online businesses usually borrow for premises?

Smaller sellers may borrow £10,000 to £40,000 to improve a unit, while larger operations moving to a bigger warehouse may need much more. Loanleaf handles enquiries from £5,000 to £2m and above. Lenders will want to see a trading record, so a newer seller may find options limited, whatever the size of the project it has in mind.

paying-a-tax-bill|ecommerce.h1: Tax bill finance for ecommerce businesses
paying-a-tax-bill|ecommerce.title: Tax Bill Finance for Ecommerce Businesses | Loanleaf
paying-a-tax-bill|ecommerce.desc: How online sellers finance VAT, import VAT and corporation tax bills that follow a peak season, with cash tied in stock. Free introduction to a broker.
paying-a-tax-bill|ecommerce.lead: Online sellers collect VAT on a rush of orders, then find the cash has gone on stock and advertising.
intro: Ecommerce cash goes out quickly. Stock is paid for before it is sold, often from overseas suppliers, and advertising is paid up front as well. When a peak such as Black Friday brings a surge of sales, VAT on that revenue is collected with every order, but the quarter’s VAT return is due after the money has been reinvested in January stock. Because many online sellers pay for stock months before it sells, the cash can be tied up exactly when the quarter’s VAT falls due.

Cross-border selling adds layers. Import VAT may be due on goods arriving into the UK, and sales to customers in other countries can raise VAT registration questions. These are matters for an accountant, but the practical effect is that tax payments can be large and well timed for the wrong moment. Short-term finance can help you meet the bill without running down stock. Sellers who also trade through marketplaces should check how and when payouts arrive, as the timing of those payments can differ from the sales date used for VAT.
uses: VAT after the peak
Pay the quarter containing Black Friday and Christmas once the money has gone on January stock and advertising.
Import VAT on a stock shipment
Meet VAT due when a large shipment arrives, before it has sold through.
Corporation tax on a growth year
Settle a bill on profits that are tied up in inventory and marketing rather than in the bank.
Payroll taxes for a growing team
Cover PAYE as the team grows faster than the accounts, especially in customer service and fulfilment.
fit: VAT and tax loans for a defined bill

A VAT and tax loan is repaid over a few months and covers a specific HMRC liability. For example, £45,000 of VAT could be spread over six months. Lenders look at VAT returns, sales history and bank statements, including marketplace and payment platform reports.
Revolving credit for repeat pressure

Ecommerce cash needs recur across the year, and a revolving credit facility lets you draw when needed and repay as sales arrive. You pay interest on what you use, and the limit remains available for the next stock order or tax date.
Merchant cash advance as an option

Sellers with high card volumes may be offered a merchant cash advance, repaid as a share of takings. It can be quick but is typically more expensive, so a broker will compare it with a term loan before suggesting it.
considerations: Stock can be slow to sell
If goods do not sell as planned, cash stays tied up while a loan is being repaid. Test repayments against a weaker sales quarter.
Cross-border VAT rules
VAT on overseas sales and imports is a specialist area. Make sure your accountant has dealt with it, so the bill you borrow against is the right figure.
Advertising spend is flexible
Marketing costs can often be reduced, which helps if sales slow. A lender may ask how adjustable your costs are.
faqs: Can an online seller get a loan to pay VAT?

Yes. VAT and tax loans are designed for this. The lender pays HMRC or releases funds so you can, and you repay in instalments. Expect to provide VAT returns, accounts and bank statements. It also helps to include a short sales summary by month, so the lender can see how the peak compares with the rest of the year.
Will lenders look at marketplace reports?

Often. Sales reports from your website, marketplaces and payment providers can show trading history. Lenders usually ask for these with accounts and bank statements, and a broker can say which are most useful. Marketplace and payment platform reports are usually the most helpful, as they show sales and payouts in a form that a lender can check.
Is a revolving facility better than a tax loan?

If tax and stock pressures keep recurring, a revolving credit facility may suit better, as it stays available. A tax loan suits one defined bill. A broker can compare both for your pattern of sales. Some sellers hold both, using the revolving facility to buy stock and keeping a separate short loan for a large, one-off HMRC liability.
What about import VAT?

Import VAT is a tax liability that can be financed in some cases. Ask your accountant whether postponed VAT accounting applies, because it can change when the VAT falls due. Rules differ depending on how goods are brought in, so confirm the position with your accountant before deciding how much to borrow.
Do start-up sellers qualify?

Loanleaf is for UK limited companies and LLPs trading six months or more with annual revenue of £50,000 or more. Newer or smaller sellers, and sole traders, are not currently eligible through Loanleaf. Lenders usually want to see a longer trading record than that, so a seller that does not yet qualify may need to wait before applying.

refurbishing-premises|professional-servi.title: Refurbishment Finance for Professional Services | Loanleaf
refurbishing-premises|professional-servi.desc: How law, accountancy, consultancy and agency firms finance office fit-outs, hybrid layouts and end-of-lease works. Get matched with a finance broker. Free.
refurbishing-premises|professional-servi.lead: Professional firms refit offices to suit hybrid working, bring in new staff or leave an old lease cleanly.
intro: A professional office is a showroom for a service nobody can see. Clients judge a firm partly on reception, meeting rooms and how organised the space feels. Since hybrid working, many firms are refitting to fewer desks and more meeting and collaboration space, with better acoustics, video-call rooms and cabling that supports it. A good fit-out can also help recruitment, because candidates compare offices, though it should be justified by how the space will actually be used.

Two lease events also drive spending. A new lease often arrives with a tenant fit-out period, and an old one ends with dilapidations, which are repairs and reinstatement owed to the landlord. Both are costs that arrive in one block against income that comes in gradually through fees, so the shape of the loan matters. Landlords sometimes offer incentives such as rent-free periods or a contribution, so ask what is on offer before deciding how much to borrow.
uses: Hybrid office layout
Replace rows of desks with bookable space, meeting rooms and quiet booths that match how the team now works.
Client meeting rooms
Fit out rooms with AV, soundproofing and glass so confidential conversations stay private and calls run smoothly.
New lease fit-out
Fit out an unfurnished floor after moving, when the landlord gives a rent-free period but not the cash for the works.
Dilapidations at lease end
Pay for repairs and reinstatement the landlord requires so the lease can end without a dispute.
fit: Unsecured loans suit fee-earning firms

An unsecured business loan, for example £75,000 over four years, is a common fit for professional firms. With no stock and few physical assets, lenders focus on fee income, recurring clients and accounts. Strong, repeat fee income helps.
Asset finance for IT and furniture
Laptops, AV equipment, servers and furniture can often be financed as assets. That keeps the refurbishment loan focused on building work, and equipment repayments follow its working life.
Match the term to the lease
A loan that runs past your lease end ties repayments to space you may leave. If the lease has five years left, a three or four year term is usually safer. A broker can help you test this.
considerations: Fees can lag the work
Billing and collection can lag a month or more, so repayments should be tested against months when WIP is high and payments are low. Lenders will look at debtor days.
Clarify what the landlord owes
Some leases cover part of a fit-out. Check what the landlord is responsible for before borrowing the whole amount.
Is a smaller office the answer?
Reducing space or moving to serviced offices may cost less than a refit. Compare the options before committing to a long loan.
faqs: Can a professional services firm borrow for an office fit-out?

Yes. Unsecured business loans are widely used, as most firms have little property or stock to offer as security. Lenders look at fee income, accounts, bank statements and the lease. The lender will usually ask for the lease and the contractor’s quotes, so it helps to have them ready when you apply.
Can I finance dilapidations?

Often, yes. Dilapidations are a business cost that can be financed, though lenders may ask for the schedule from the landlord. A broker can advise on how a lender will view it. It also helps to have the schedule of dilapidations or the quote for works from the landlord’s surveyor, as lenders like to see a defined figure.
Will lenders consider my work in progress?

They look at accounts and cash flow, and WIP shows what you are due to bill. Debtor days matter too, since they show how quickly fees convert into cash. Some firms also share their pipeline and recent billing, which can help a lender see that fee income should continue through the repayment period.
Is asset finance useful for office technology?

It can be. IT, AV equipment and furniture are physical assets, and financing them separately keeps the main loan smaller and spreads cost across their useful life. A broker can suggest how to split the costs between the building work and the equipment so each is matched to the right facility.
How much do firms usually borrow?
